title: Ang 705–710: Jaitsri ki Var
tomorrow: what do you say to someone you're about to miss?

lines: A VAR: A BALLAD OF HEROES.
cards: Stadium chants, a walk-out song, the anthem before the game: people sing about strength. In Punjabi, a var is a ballad, a form known for songs of heroes.
On ang 705 Guru Arjan writes one, Jaitsri ki Var, and the hero isn't a warrior at all. It opens: perfect at the beginning, perfect in the middle, perfect at the end, the Lord of all.

teach.b: A var moves in steps. Each stanza is a pauri, a step on a stair, and in the Granth short saloks often come before it. Guru Arjan keeps that shape and turns it toward God.

The opening salok, in paraphrase: perfect at the beginning, in the middle and at the end; the saints remember the One who is everywhere; Nanak says, the Lord of the world destroys sin. Listen to the strength in that.

It isn't one big moment of winning. It's a line that holds from first to last, steady as a beat you could tap. Then, after the ballad, one hymn by Ravidas, on ang 710, and it sounds like the opposite.
In paraphrase: Lord, I know nothing. My mind has been sold into the world's hands. Put the two side by side and they fit.

The ballad says the strength runs from beginning to end, and it isn't ours to supply. Ravidas says honestly: I can't hold this up by myself. The hero's song and the humble confession meet in one place.
The hero of this ballad doesn't flex.
Its strength is that the beat never drops.

how: Vars in the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan's Jaitsri ki Var among them, are sung in kirtan stanza by stanza, each pauri with its saloks.

games.q: your team is down at halftime. the captain says she alone will carry the second half. a teammate says Guru Arjan's ballad would put it another way. how?
o: big speeches are pride; real strength never says a word.
the strength that holds runs start to finish, and isn't hers alone.
she should admit the game is lost and stop pretending.
games.why: the ballad's strength runs beginning, middle and end, and Ravidas admits he can't hold it up himself. strength is shared, and steady.

practice: Tap a slow, steady beat on your knee with one hand, and let your breath find it: in on one tap, out on the next. Partway through, let the hand go still and keep listening for the beat that's still there, your breath, your pulse.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: var, a ballad in stanzas; Jaitsri ki Var is Guru Arjan's (ang 705–710).

carryVoice: Strength: the beat that holds from the first line to the last, even when you know nothing. Fifteen-thirty, in rhythm.
